handoff.reason: Systematic review specifically on GI side effects of MCT consumption -- useful standing safety/tolerability reference for any oral MCT recommendation.

identity_notes: MCT oil's retrieval set is dominated by a large PARENTERAL/INTRAVENOUS cluster -- MCT/LCT lipid emulsions used in parenteral nutrition, propofol anesthetic formulations (MCT is a common excipient), and IV fat infusion/tolerance studies -- all rejected not_this_route since these are intravenous, not oral supplement use. A second cluster is rare chylous/lymphatic conditions (chylothorax, chylous ascites, chylopericardium, intestinal lymphangiectasia): individual case reports were rejected off_topic as purely descriptive of the underlying disease, and broader treatment-option reviews for these conditions were rejected not_intervention since MCT-diet-specific extractable data was not confirmed in the retrieved abstracts, even though MCT diet is understood to be standard adjunct therapy for these conditions in clinical practice. A third recurring confound is generic 'ketogenic diet' and Alzheimer's/epilepsy reviews that do not name MCT specifically in the title or visible abstract -- classic ketogenic diets are LCT/fat-based, and only a subset are the MCT-variant, so these were rejected not_intervention unless MCT was explicitly confirmed as the reviewed intervention (in which case they were kept, e.g. 36716045's network meta-analysis explicitly comparing 'medium chain triglyceride diet' as its own arm). A fourth pattern is MCT used purely as a delivery excipient/solvent for an unrelated active (licorice flavonoids, cannabidiol, topical antifungal nanocarriers) -- these were rejected off_topic/not_intervention since MCT itself is not the tested variable. Among genuine oral MCT trials, the most consistent and repeated evidence clusters are: acute satiety/energy-intake effects (generally positive vs. LCT), sarcopenia/frailty in elderly adults (a coherent trial program: 27075909 combination, then 31334544 and 35122097 isolating MCT alone), cognitive function in MCI/Alzheimer's via mild ketosis induction (multiple positive meta-analyses: 31870908, 37248908, 36633304, 36273115, 38715705), and exercise/endurance performance (mixed results, often when MCT is combined with carbohydrate or structured with EPA). Two reviews (41001501, 41097203) cover 'exogenous ketones/ketosis' broadly, of which MCT is one source among ketone esters and salts; these are flagged related_form_differs since MCT-specific results are not isolated within them.
